question: If $F(x)$ is an anti-derivative of $f(x)$, show that $\int_0^{\pi} f(\pi-x)dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(x)dx$ and verify for $f(x)=\sin x$.
explanation:
Let $I=\int_0^{\pi} f(\pi-x)dx$.

Substitute $u=\pi-x$ so $du=-dx$.

When $x=0$, $u=\pi$ and when $x=\pi$, $u=0$.

Thus $I=\int_{\pi}^0 f(u)(-du)=\int_0^{\pi} f(u)du$.

Hence $\int_0^{\pi} f(\pi-x)dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(x)dx$.

Verification for $f(x)=\sin x$:

$\int_0^{\pi}\sin(\pi-x)dx = \int_0^{\pi}\sin x dx = [-\cos x]_0^{\pi}=2$.

options.C:
$\int_0^{\pi} f(\pi-x)dx = \int_0^{\pi} f(x)dx$
For $f(x)=\sin x$, both integrals equal $2$
